title: The Chemist Who Invented Synthetic Indigo
event_summary: In 1897, BASF began commercial production of synthetic indigo dye based on Adolf von Baeyer's chemical synthesis, perfected for industrial scale by Karl Heumann's process. Within a decade, this single chemical achievement obliterated the centuries-old indigo plantation economy of Bengal, Bihar, and other tropical regions, destroying the livelihoods of millions of Indian farmers who had been coerced into cultivating natural indigo under brutal colonial contracts. The collapse of indigo farming became one of the critical economic grievances that fueled early Indian nationalist movements, including Gandhi's famous 1917 Champaran Satyagraha.
why_forgotten: The event sits awkwardly between chemistry, colonial economics, and political history, so no single discipline claims it as central. European histories celebrate von Baeyer's 1905 Nobel Prize as pure scientific triumph without acknowledging the devastation it caused. Indian histories foreground the political resistance rather than the chemical catalyst that made it necessary.
why_it_matters: Synthetic indigo was arguably the first case where industrial chemistry destroyed an entire global agricultural commodity overnight, establishing a pattern repeated with synthetic rubber, fertilizers, and countless other products. The Champaran campaign it provoked became Gandhi's first major political action in India, helping birth the modern nonviolent resistance movement. Today, every pair of blue jeans owes its color to this synthetic process, while debates about synthetic versus natural dyes echo in contemporary sustainability movements.
